en: Composed by the Tang Dynasty Tiantai monk Zhìràn.
Under the heading "The Equality of the Seed" (Zǐděngzǐ), he sets forth two topical gates. Regarding the statement, "Because the seed is equal, the mind is equal":
first, to clarify that the seed is equal means that because there is nothing that is not the seed, the mind must necessarily be equal; as for that mind...

Because they treat their children equally, their minds are equal; since the mind is the nature of the mind, it is the Buddha-nature. Because all are their children, their minds are without partiality; because the wealth and Dharma are further abundant, their minds are equal.
Regarding the phrase "chariots and so forth": first, it clarifies that what is bestowed by the Equal Intent is non-dual; therefore, it is called "equal.
It merely indicates that whatever is practiced is none other than the wondrous vehicle; it is simply because their nature is identical that the meaning of being bestowed is equal.

Regarding the phrase "and yet," it subsequently resolves the doubts concerning the chariots and so forth by means of the sons and so forth. Since it has already been stated that there are "chariots and so forth," why are they each bestowed?
Because past training was not uniform and their respective stations were not identical, what is taught here is none other than the One Vehicle.
Why is this? If one person were not included in the entirety, they could not be called a "son" or the like.

Furthermore, it is said that one's original practice should pervade all dharmas; if even a single thing were not bestowed, it could not be called a "gift" or the like. This refers to form and mind, the adverse and the favorable, the environment and its inhabitants, practice and principle, cause and effect, self and other, delusion and awakening, small and great, wisdom and merit. Therefore, we know that "equal bestowal" simply means opening up those of the three vehicles and six paths so that there is nothing that is not the One Suchness. Thus, every suchness universally encompasses, universally possesses, and universally enters. Among all sentient beings, who lacks their share in the four-directional site of enlightenment? Who does not possess the Great Vehicle within the Dharma-realm to be fully delivered? It is merely because they await the proper time and conditions that it is so; therefore, it is only until today that it is said, "I bestow upon each of you."

Regarding the phrase "horizontal pervasion" (*heng-zhou*) and so forth: the three truths of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are neither horizontal nor vertical. Although there is no such distinction of horizontal or vertical, it is convenient to speak of them as "horizontal" because the Dharma-realm is all-pervasive; it is convenient to speak of them as "vertical" because the three truths have distinct names. One should reflect that they are non-dual and mutually manifesting, which can be seen through contemplation.
Regarding the "four analytical knowledges" (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ), they are: dharma, artha, nirukti, and pratibhāna; these are largely the same as the seven analytical knowledges.
"Dharma" refers to the unimpeded discernment of the names and designations of all phenomena, and the discernment of the three vehicles without violating the nature of reality (dharmatā).
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the thorough penetration of the meaning of all phenomena, knowing that all meanings enter into the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

"Phrasing" (*vyañjana*) refers to the adornment of speech and names; according to what is appropriate, it enables understanding for all sentient beings—those of different regions and species, whether few or many, broad or narrow, those on various paths, male or female, and those who hear through the various teachings and gateways of the three periods or nine periods of time. All such listeners understand completely.

Eloquence means being able to speak of all syllables within a single syllable, all words within a single word, and all phenomena within a single phenomenon; whatever is spoken is invariably true, and one teaches the eighty-four thousand [teachings] according to the inclinations of the faculties of beings.
Regarding the "Four Immeasurables," they take the Four Truths as their object because there are two types of suffering and two types of happiness.
They are fundamentally the inconceivable Brahma-conduct; thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"If compassion is neither existent nor non-existent, and neither existent-nor-non-existent—such compassion is called the Tathāgata’s compassion. Therefore, the compassion of the [first] three truths subsumes the four universal [compassions].
The Four Great Vows and the Four Means of Integration are both categorized according to their objects (*ālambana*), which distinguishes them from other sutras.
The "Four Great Vows" are fully detailed in the first and fifth fascicles of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).
These Four Great Vows are identical to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) discussed previously.
The "Four Means of Integration" (catvāri saṃgrahavastūni) are briefly explained as in the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

The supernormal powers (abhijñā) and the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) both take the "objectless" (anālambana) as their basis, as clarified in the section on the Truth of the Path of Non-action (anabhisaṃskāra-mārgasatya) in the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
"Quán" refers to embroidered robes.
"Yán" refers to the robe worn over the crown by the Son of Heaven, specifically that which hangs down at the front and back;
this is not the intended meaning here, for it should instead be written as "yán" (筵), meaning a spread mat.
Regarding "contemplation, refinement, perfuming, and cultivation," their specific names and characteristics are fully set forth in the *Dharmadhātusthāna*.

As for the "meditative objects of śamatha and vipaśyanā," both the *Mysterious* (Xuan) and the *Text on the Stages of the Sages* (Wen ding sheng xing) state that these are cultivated because they constitute the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); thus, their superior functions remain inexhaustible within the meditations of the fruition stage.
Regarding the statement in the *Danzhen* that "zhī'áng" refers to the pillow outside the carriage: when the carriage stops, one must prop it up with this pillow for fear that it might tip over;
hence it is called "zhī'áng. "Zhī" means to support.
"Ang" means "to raise. Regarding the phrase "for example, movement and stillness are mutually identical":

when a carriage is in motion, the axle is at rest; when the carriage stops, the axle is in use. At the time of use, it is constantly still; at the time of rest, it is constantly moving. The same applies to the substantial entity and its function.

The dharma-nature of the fruit arising from its own cause is immovable; thus, like the wind that reaches its destination without shifting, it arrives in stillness. The myriad practices are without action, and the manifold wisdoms cannot perceive them; this is the non-duality of the three virtues.
It is simply because the three are identical with the one.
Regarding the "pillow within the carriage": the three jewels of wisdom, conduct, and body are like a pillow; it is thus that one finds rest in the principle of the Dharma-principle.
Regarding the phrase "red light" and so forth: it is called "non-conceptual" because there is no other dharma intervening; since light is used as a metaphor for wisdom, it is termed "wisdom-light.
Because vermilion is a pure purple without intermixture, red is used here to represent light that is free from admixture.
The *Nanshan Zhujing yin* states:
"In the Western Regions, there are no wooden pillows; instead, all are made of red hide with cotton wool stuffed inside, used for reclining and sleeping.
They are red and glossy.

The white ox is treated in three parts: first, its functional capacity is clarified; second, from "White is... onwards, its essential nature and qualities are expounded; third, from "Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness... onwards, its modes of practice are discussed.

Regarding the first passage: the Prajñā attained through cultivation can guide one toward the provisional and the middle; since there is no object among the truths of the three teachings that it does not reach its ultimate limit, it is said to "arrive.
This name is common [to other contexts], and thus its essential nature must be distinguished.

Next, within the section on the qualities of the essence (*tattva-guṇa*), it says: "White is the basis of color. Because the fundamental essence is free from defilement, it is called "primordially pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*); because cultivation accords with this nature, it is called "concordant" (*anuloma*).

The phrase "endowment of essence" (*tǐjù*) and so forth reveals perfect wisdom. Since the essence of delusion is fundamentally pure, cultivation is discussed in terms of its nature; this is termed "non-defilement" (*bùrǎn*). This signifies that it is internally full and externally pure.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Again, the four foundations of mindfulness" explains the modes of activity (*ākāra*) by way of their objects. Here, "mindfulness" refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), and "foundations" refer to the objects (*viṣaya*). The four contemplations contemplate each foundation, and these foundations are contemplated as a unified whole. Just as when something is entirely white it is considered the body, so too this object of contemplation—where goodness is fully perfected and evil is exhausted—can be likened to right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*).

Because this is accomplished, it further causes the mental application of desire and thought to become a single-mindedly neutral supernormal power (*abhijñā*). Since the transformations proceed without interruption, occurring spontaneously and eternally, and because going and staying are sovereign, it is called "according with one's intent. Other dharmas may be illustrated by what is explained in the *Mārga-varga* (Chapter on the Path).
Question:

In this context, the great chariots and other gifts are bestowed upon the sons; yet, once the sons have received them, they have only just begun their first stage of abiding, remaining even now at the level of conceptual observation and practice (*nāma-manasikāra*). How can these be explained solely in terms of the meaning of the fruit (*phala*)?
Answer:

By means of realization, one demonstrates the distinctions among the practices of various people; by clarifying the causes and so forth, one cites phenomena to reveal the principle. Therefore, it is simply shown that "the practice you all engage in is the Bodhisattva path," for the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in these three aspects. Thus, this is the bestowal of the principle.
The "bestowal of the stages of practice" (*caryā-bhūmi*) and so forth is precisely the bestowal of the fruit (*phala*).
Since the principle of the fruit exists within practice, it can only be called a "bestowal" when that practice is present; how could the principle-fruit itself be bestowed upon sentient beings?

Regarding the term "attendants" (*pārṣada*), according to the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), they correspond to the distinction between the primary and the auxiliary within the body of the chariot, and to the oxen as the means of attainment. This corresponds in meaning to the two natures and one essence (*dvaya-svabhāva eka-tattva*) cultivated in practice; furthermore, this one essence possesses the three qualities of height, breadth, and non-duality. Here, the term "attendants" differs in wording but is identical in meaning to the "retinue" (*anuyātra*) mentioned in the verse. "Retinue" (*anuyātra*) means to advance or to lead forward.
"Attendants" refers to those who serve at one's left and right;
"servants" refers to those of lower rank.
Now, those who practice the Mahāyāna should examine their own minds: do they correspond to, or differ from, what is listed in this scriptural passage?
If a single phrase were sufficient, what phrase would it be?
If one phrase is enough, why are multiple phrases required?
Could it be that the Buddha spoke erroneously, merely indulging in florid rhetoric and laboriously arraying ritual procedures to delude Kāśyapa?

This great Arhat has long served as the head of the Saṅgha; for over forty years he did not receive the true transformation. Only upon hearing the skillful means that universally extol the two wisdoms, and having briefly heard the revelation of the truth, his attachments were shaken and doubts arose. While his mind was still hesitant, he earnestly made three requests. Having heard extensively the five Buddhas’ tenfold opening of the provisional, he further observed Śāriputra’s threefold physical, verbal, and mental realization, the eight classes of beings citing precedents, the fourfold assembly repaying their debt of gratitude, and the Tathāgata’s concluding summary which clearly bestowed the prediction. Although through these repeated events his past seeds had not yet blossomed, as soon as he heard of the "Great Vehicle," he was ready to receive the prediction.

Therefore, know that while this vehicle’s method of contemplation is complete, it still preserves a concise outline consisting of ten contemplations. If one were to extensively elaborate upon its practical aspects, how could they ever be fully prepared?
By not providing separate explanations, one immediately awakens to non-arising; compared to what follows, this is termed "middling," yet relative to what precedes it, it remains superior.

If this analogy of the chariot were merely a hollow statement, it would imply that the Buddha was guilty of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), or that the compilers of the canon were at fault for interpolating extraneous material, or that the translators were culpable for mixing different traditions.

Conversely, if there is a valid basis for the correspondence, then the conduct and rituals [of the Great Vehicle] can serve as a model; why then should one suddenly and entirely abandon the study of its grand vision? Having lost the great standard, one cannot follow a minor path; if both the great and the small are lost, one fears falling into heterodox ways. Riding a broken donkey carriage, toward what destination shall one proceed?
Regarding the phrase “like the fruit-stage where merit and wisdom are perfected”: this means that the principle of practice has reached its ultimate limit;

merit is the fulfillment of practice, while wisdom is the penetration of principle. Because the virtues of one’s own practice are complete, there is internal sufficiency; because the virtues for transforming others are fully present, they overflow externally. Because they pervade all phenomena, wealth is immeasurable; because both types of virtue are possessed, it is called “various.”

Regarding the enumeration of the two treasuries (piṭakas): because practice accords with principle and principle relies upon practice, they must mutually encompass one another to be worthy of equal bestowal.

The passage beginning with "All" cites scriptural evidence for these two treasuries: if one does not understand the treasury of principle concerning the aggregates (skandha) and bases (āyatana), one merely practices the treasury of conduct consisting of the various perfections (pāramitā) in vain.

Regarding the phrase "all destinies" (*sarvagati*), the text appears in the "Chapter on Setting Out" (*Prasthāna-parivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. "Destiny" (*gati*) here means "entering"; that is, all phenomena enter into a single phenomenon. Just as it is with this one phenomenon, so it is with all phenomena; thus, the principle of practice fully encompasses all phenomena.
"All dharmas tend toward the opening and closing of literary forms," as cited in the second fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
Following the passage "practicing this principle for oneself," the text next explains "overflowing."

First, the practice and principle are directly summarized; next, from the section on "True Wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*) downward, the capacity to guide and illuminate represents the meaning of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) attained through cultivation.
Because it reaches the ultimate fruit and benefits sentient beings, it is called "overflowing."
Although there are these two interpretations, the Buddha’s wisdom does not differ [between them].
Within the "equality of mind" (*cittasamatā*), there are likewise two [meanings], but it is simply called "mind" (*citta*) because the mind is the son of the Buddha.
When all three meanings are present together, it is designated as "equality of mind."
First is wealth, second is having sons, and third is impartiality.
Therefore, the mind is equanimous; furthermore, one should state that the mind is equanimous because all are his sons.
His immeasurable wealth signifies the fulfillment of his own practice.
"All are children" means there is no partiality; it is because the conditions for transformation have matured.

Regarding the phrase "if wealthy," the text uses inequality as a counter-argument to explain equality: because wealth and children are mutually lacking, the mind becomes unequal. One should know that it is not the children or the wealth themselves that are unequal; this is merely a provisional reliance on the teachings of the past. Thus, in the partial teachings of the past, both the Master who transforms and the capacity of those to be transformed were deficient. For example, the Masters of those two teachings were poor in the wealth of Dharma, and therefore they could not be called "wealthy";
they did not know of the eternal abiding [of the Buddha-nature], and thus they could not regard all beings as their children.

Even if one were to grant that the teaching of the Separate Vehicle (Bie-jiao) designates [the practitioners] as "sons," its application would still not be universal; thus, it too would be partial. Since they are mutually deficient, it can be understood that they are equally lacking.

Although the path of the teaching (jiao-dao) in the Separate Vehicle is said to consist of "sons" in both senses, these two meanings are still absent; however, in the path of realization (zheng-dao), they are naturally equal to those of the Shared Vehicle (Tong-jiao) and so forth without deficiency. One may infer this by applying the same logic to the subsequent explanations of "sons" and so on.

Therefore, in this sutra, there is no dharma other than the one reality; all sentient beings are my children. Since even the conditional causes include scattered virtues, and the seeds of enlightenment universally encompass a single phrase, it truly does not abandon even those in the Avīci hell—only then can it be called the teaching of "all."

Therefore, within the *Xuanwen* (Text on the Profound), regarding the exposition of benefits, it is established that the sequence of the introduction, the main body, and the circulation shall endure eternally in the future; this can be understood by applying the same principle to King Śubhavyūha, Devadatta, the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging, and the Dragon Girl.

Moreover, how could the words "should be" be restricted to the four realms of existence, and how could the teachings "according to suitability" fail to distinguish between those who are compliant and those who are contrary?
These are the general principles [of the Buddha's teaching].
Therefore, one should know that the statement regarding the "equality of mind" among you disciples does not refer merely to the four great śrāvakas.
Therefore, all dharmas are treasured within him, treating all as his children without partiality.
The section beginning with "Now, the seven treasures" explains three meanings.

First, it clarifies the abundance of wealth; regarding the phrase "teaching and practice," this refers to the correspondence between the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teacher, spoken here from the perspective of the benefits found in the extant text.
Next, the section beginning with "each and every" clarifies that these sons are without partiality.

The term "each and every" is used because they are all sons; "without distinction" is used because there is no partiality. Granting each an equal share of one [portion] is precisely the opening of the provisional means (*upāya*).
Next, to explain the meaning of "each," the passage cites Śāriputra and others; because their original practices were different, they each equally enter into reality, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also the Vaipulya and Prajñā [sūtras]," this refers to the fact that, according to the Dharma, the faculties, powers, and mastery have already been opened. For those with dull faculties who obtain benefit from the teachings of skillful means at the beginning of the two flavors (the *Śrāvaka* and *Pratyekabuddha* stages), they obtain benefit therein. Since the various positions and dharmas differ in many ways, all are opened by means of reality according to their respective positions.

Regarding the phrase "therefore" (*so yi*), it explains what follows concerning the "sons" (*zi*) and so forth. As for the expression "both" (*liang*), one should simply say "sons"; the inclusion of "both" is likely an error.

If even Wenju and Cai and others are compared to his sons, and even those who merely share the same residence are compared to his sons, how much more so are his own sons—those who were originally of one family and are now subjects of one state? How much more so, indeed, are his sons!
The term "one land" refers to the Land of Quiescent Light (*Sukhāvatī*).
Since its universal benefit for the entire *dharmadhātu* is inexhaustible in principle, how much more so for those who form karmic connections within the Land of Common Dwelling?
This passage uses the broad category to illustrate the abbreviated individual.
In the section beginning with "Next, the explanation," the text properly clarifies the "sons" and so forth, further using those who are "not sons" as a point of comparison.

Regarding the term "not sons": this is used provisionally to disparage the direct cause (the *dharmakāya* nature) as being distinct from the conditional and responsive causes (*pratyaya* and *upāya*), and thus it is depreciatively termed "not."

Since all sentient beings within the aggregates (*skandha*) are impartial, how much more so those with whom one has established a karmic connection? Therefore, in relation to the principle of non-referential compassion (*apratigha-maitrī*), there is no one who is not one's own child; this is merely spoken of in terms of the provisional manifestations of the transformative ritual (*vyañjana*). Furthermore, those from previous lives with whom no connection was established are considered "non-children" only because the Tathāgata constantly provides for them as his own children, yet they do not return [to him]. Because non-referential compassion universally covers all, it is said that he "provides for all. Since the good and evil of humans and devas are identical to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the father’s fruit-cart is itself the child’s principle-cart; it is only to open their emotional attachments that these are provisionally called "equal gifts."

The vehicle for sentient beings is inexhaustible and never-ending; because it is not exhausted, it is not depleted; because it is not depleted, it is without partiality. It opens for those who look in confusion, yet its fundamental nature is not closed even to those who have awakened.

Regarding the phrase "even those without conditions are saved": the children of the Perfect Cause who have previously established a connection with the Trace are brought to maturity and liberation; as for the children of the True Cause who have not yet established a connection, seeds are sown for them. Therefore, it is said that "even they are saved."

Therefore, using the sower as an analogy for those who have previously established karmic connections, [the text] explains that what was not in vain. Regarding the initial question posed by the Buddha: "Originally you permitted only three [refuges], yet now you grant one; is this not false?"
Because he wished to lead Śāriputra to realize the ultimate truth, he questioned him with what was illusory.
His initial answer avoided the immediate peril, yet it was not false within the context of the explanation.
The *Sūtra* states, "If one were to preserve one's body and life," which fully cites both body and life as a metaphor for being rescued and delivered.

The intention is this: if one fully enters the life-force of wisdom within emptiness via the fivefold Dharma-body of the Hīnayāna, then one has already attained that which has been cherished since of old; how much more so, then, is the fundamental greatness of the skillful means for rescuing suffering from the burning house?
Question:

The sutra text uses "rescue" (*bajì*) as a metaphor for both body and life; logically, rescue should be used to illustrate the great in contrast to the small—namely, life versus body. Why, then, does the commentary (*shūwén*) not employ "rescue," but instead state that "life is heavy and the body is light," using the five aggregates of the Hīnayāna as the "body" to illustrate the true wisdom (*saddharma-prajñā*) of the Mahāyāna as "life"?
Why is a small body contrasted with a great life?
Answer:

This is a figurative explanation through mutual comparison. Within the "small," one takes untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) as life; the Mahāyāna itself possesses the equal Dharma-body (*samatā-dharmakāya*). Thus, it is appropriate to employ the bodies and lives of the small and the great as a point of contrast.
The phrase “exempt from the eight sufferings” below concludes by directing the focus toward the gravity of life and the lightness of the body.

One should understand that one borrows a small life for the sake of a great life; initially, one uses the small to sustain the five aggregates, which is already a precious attainment. How much more so when the expedient teaching within the burning house takes the small as the basis for the great, and one now attains the great—is this not anything but true?
The fivefold dharma-body of the Hīnayāna is fully detailed in the *Abhidharmakośa*, and so forth.
The passage beginning with "How much more so for twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas" refers to past causes.
While the Sūtra uses only the present world as a burning house by way of analogy, the Commentary adds the reference to the great [suffering] of the past to provide an explanation.
The phrase "from the 'Perfect Cause Accomplishment'" points toward the present result.

Regarding the expression "not contradicting the original intent," this describes the Elder’s original intention: whether small or great, both possess an original core. Since the Great Root serves as the root while the Small Root is not the root, even if one grants that the small does not accord [with the great], there is still no contradiction; how much less so when it further accords with the great—how could it possibly contradict the original intent?
If such a small amount of wealth and a minor rank were not false, how much more so when one receives a great position that surpasses the past? How could this not be the original intention?

One can thus know with certainty that the Tathāgata’s fundamental teaching was never one of mere minor transformation; therefore, as for wealth, it merely spares one from the poverty of the分段 (pudgala-bheda) realm, while as for rank, it transcends the lowliness of the two deaths (dvimaraṇa). Since both meanings are simultaneously fulfilled, what contradiction could there be?
It is merely a minor matter and not ultimate; there was no need to grant it further, which is why it is said that he "did not grant" it.

Regarding the passage from "Originally knowing there are no three" to "original mind," this clarifies the intention behind not granting it: since it was not his original intent in the past, he does not grant it now. The *Sūtra* says, "By means of skillful means, he causes them to emerge," and the Commentary says, "Causing them not to fall into evil. Because he causes them not to fall, he uses skillful means to cause them to emerge; because he uses skillful means to cause them to emerge, he causes them not to fall into evil—thus, these are one and the same meaning.

Regarding the phrase "linking the preceding" and so forth: when both conclusions are explained together as being "similar," the phrasing appears to link them exclusively, yet in principle they must be possessed simultaneously. Because the two wheels are distinct, their respective objects of opposition differ; therefore, the two wheels are borrowed to resolve the two conclusions.
"Self-substance" (*svabhāva*) refers to the Land of Real Reward (*sambhoga-kṣetra*).

This is a designation established by the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* based on its causes: namely, the collection of conditioned conditions is the cause of the Land of Common Residence; the collection of unconditioned conditions is the cause of the Land of Expedient Means; and the collection of self-substance conditions is the cause of the Land of Real Reward, also termed the collection of Dharma-realm conditions.

In this commentary, the first two [realms] still follow the traditional practice of establishing their names based on the fruit (*phala*), while the latter one follows that [tradition] by establishing its designation based on the cause (*hetu*).

Regarding the phrase "all are the places of retribution for wondrous form and wondrous mind": since it is said that [the Buddha] is the father of all worlds, we know that the three lands are all places of retribution for the form and mind realized through the Path. Since the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhā*) is all-pervasive, Vairocana is likewise equal; since all bodies are identical in measure to the Dharma-body, all lands are no different from the Land of Tranquil Light. This can be understood by analogy with an image and a mirror, or with rice and a vessel. All sentient beings without exception possess these; yet because their retributive fruits are not yet fulfilled, they remain entirely within delusion. Due to delusion, their physical aggregates are confined to that vast void; when fulfillment is attained, they are immediately equal in measure to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As for those who respond to the three lands, this is spoken according to the perspective of transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-karma*); hence it is said that the "places" are equal.

Regarding the phrase "In all fears" and so forth: for the time being, speaking in terms of causes and effects within the realm [of saṃsāra], since these sons are objects of fear, it is said that they are "forever exhausted."
That which is abandoned is coarse, while the principle by which it is abandoned is ultimate; therefore, it is said that there are "immeasurable knowledge and vision," and so forth.

Some explain this by citing the abandonment of the five fears in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*); however, these two have no connection whatsoever. The former does not reach the level of the Buddhas, and the latter falls below the transcendence of the realms (*dhātu-vyatikrama*); such is the nature of their respective interpretations.
Regarding the phrase "However, in the analogy, fear appears before one," etc., the previous passage stated, "Immediately becoming greatly terrified, he thinks thus," and so forth.
The subsequent mention of "attachment" is a further explanation of what was seen.

Regarding the fact that what was previously not perceived now appears before us: the earlier statement, "Sentient beings are submerged within it," and so forth, is a brief presentation followed by an explanation in detail.

As for the phrase "extracting them from suffering" appearing later, it occurs immediately after this passage, where it says, "I am the father of sentient beings; I should extract them from their hardships and calamities," and so on.

Regarding the passage from "One should uproot their suffering" to "the power of compassion": Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) first proceeds by uprooting defilement, while Great Loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī) bestows great bliss; therefore, loving-kindness follows the intention of transformation, whereas compassion follows the application of utility.

Regarding the phrase "The preceding analogy contains an exhortation," this explains the meaning of the presence or absence of the analogy and the Dharma; that is, the lateral and the primary are mutually identical, which means their essence is fundamentally the same.

Moreover, since these two passages are both *siddhi* (establishments), one should know that the fundamental purpose of exhorting toward good is to cause the severance of evil, and the fundamental purpose of severing evil is to exhort toward good.
Question:
Since their essence is identical, why is it necessary to establish two [categories], first demonstrating their mutual absence and then their mutual identity?

Answer: Because the gateways are distinct, there are two; because their essence is identical, they are one. Although exhortation (*samādāpanā*) is itself admonition (*anuśāsana*), it is the admonition within the context of exhortation; and although admonition is itself exhortation, it is the exhortation within the context of admonition. Therefore, while each gateway remains distinct, this does not hinder their unity in essence.
Question:
If that is so, what flaw would there be in the principle of abolishing [the practice] through a single gate?
Answer:

If one is well-versed in both gates, even one gate is sufficient; however, if even one gate is abandoned, both meanings will be deficient. Moreover, the father’s earnestness was such that he first exhorted and then warned; perhaps at times these were adapted differently to suit various capacities, yet they were not distinct in their timing, for together they accomplished a single purpose.

Regarding the statement "my births are exhausted" and so forth: these four knowledges of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are possessed by all arhats. Alternatively, for those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) who have not yet attained the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), the first and last two knowledges are now characterized by non-reliance, while the middle two knowledges are characterized by the absence of seeking; this is because future existence constitutes the very basis [of seeking].

If birth has been exhausted and there is no further dependence on the future, and the two intermediate knowledges have exhausted the causes of the three realms, one is said to be "one who has accomplished what was to be done" (kṛtārtha) and so forth; therefore, it is said that "there is nothing to seek."

Regarding the statement, "There are four stages above, namely the true, the semblance, and so forth," the stage of the worthy (ārya) is combined into two, as are the two stages of the noble ones (ārya). Now, following the previous classification of external worldlings (pṛthagjana), these are likewise reduced to one for the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) and one for the wisdoms of reflection and cultivation (cintāmayī- and bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).

Regarding the statement, “The Pratyekabuddha is one who practices according to the Dharma”: for the time being, this is said in contrast to the Śrāvaka, who relies upon the teachings; thus, while the Pratyekabuddha contemplates the Dharma for himself, he must necessarily realize it through his own direct experience. The Śrāvaka, however, possesses both faith and the Dharma. That he possesses both faith and the Dharma is as cited in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan), which quotes passages from the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts.

Regarding the phrase "having heard little of the Dharma," this refers to those Pratyekabuddhas who, having heard the teachings, fell among the Śrāvakas; they are also said to have "heard little" because their realization was based solely on faith.
As for the passage from "this gate" to "not a Buddha" and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There was once a practitioner who asked the Buddha:"
"Venerable One!
Did the Buddha create the twelve links of dependent origination?
The Buddha said:
"I did not do it.
He asked again:
"Did someone else do it?"
The Buddha said:
"It was not made by anyone else; whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, this fundamental nature exists.
Now, there are four ways of answering questions, and this is an answer of definitive certainty (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*).

If one were to set forth the details of the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) regarding the truths and conditions, they would be complete as found in the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*; the text of the *Xuan* [the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*] provides only a brief summary.

Regarding the phrase "but [they] combined," among these four, two are primary and two are secondary; one should know that [the sons] sought the carriage because they wished to avoid calamity, and they rejoiced because of the equal distribution.

Regarding the statement, "The gate has three meanings": among the three gates, the specific emergence is the gate, while the entry is established as its meaning. From one form-and-mind entering another form-and-mind, the gate takes "passing through" as its meaning; however, it is not yet called "entry" until there is the act of entering from one into another. While it is spoken of as "entry," in reality, nothing comes from without.

"Regarding 'if it is produced by [the author],' this must encompass the Tripiṭaka; here, we establish the teaching of the Shared Vehicle (Pāryāptika-yāna) as that which is elucidated, because the teachings elucidated by these two vehicles are identical.
Regarding 'if it is according to a distinct meaning,' this refers to those who rely on a distinct principle."
Regarding the term "that which is expressed" (*so-ch'üan*), the intent is to clarify that the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*pieh-chiao*) is not established [independently].

Although the sutra speaks of "teaching," it must necessarily be contrasted with "principle" (*li*); therefore, we know that although the Separate Teaching expresses a distinct principle, it is nonetheless not a separate vehicle or door, but merely receives the name "separate" in contrast to the Shared Canon (*t'ung-tsang*).
It is called "distinct" because it relies on a distinct principle.

Regarding the beginning of the sequence, both those of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings alike emerge from the burning house; since they are identical in their emergence from the house, they may still be termed "shared."
The initial realization is also identical to the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles; therefore, it may also be said that one attains the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

The three virtues are fully explained in the "Three Dharmas" section of the *Xuánwén* (Mysterious Texts) and in the third fascicle of the *Zhǐguān* (Cessation and Contemplation), in the section on "Revealing the Essence."

Regarding the statement, "This explanation differs slightly from the previous one": previously it was said that the intention did not lie in the three [vehicles], whereas now it is said that the original intent was to bestow the Great [Vehicle]. Although there is a slight difference, the names differ while the meaning remains the same.
Regarding the phrase "there was a great house," some say that it refers to one of the three realms (tridhātu) as a representative unit, hence the term "one.
Others provide an extensive enumeration of categories based on the distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties.
Regarding the statement, "The three realms have been so for a long time, without beginning," a question is raised:

If it is said that [the realms] are without beginning from the perspective of their causes, yet from the perspective of their dependent retribution they were recently formed during the Bhadrakalpa starting from the first dhyāna downward, how can they be said to be without beginning?
Answer:

Sentient beings have possessed the causes for the three realms since beginningless time; because the seeds of delusion have not been extinguished, they are said to be "beginningless. Therefore, while the environment and its inhabitants undergo destruction and subsequent formation, even the Fourth Dhyāna and the Formless Realm—though free from calamitous destruction—are nonetheless characterized by the mutual conditioning of cause and effect, all being beginningless and impermanent.
Nevertheless, it is ultimately not as convenient to explain the principle by means of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
Regarding the phrase "continuing moment by moment" and so forth: because they continue in succession, they are high; because they are impermanent, they are precarious.
"Consciousness as the structural framework" means that it governs the entire body, just as the ridgepole and rafters stand up to form a house.
"Ruined and split apart" means that it is shattered and torn from top to bottom.
"Di" (褫) means the appearance of stripping off clothes.

Regarding the "two interpretations of contemplating the mind through causes and conditions": as it is said, "the head is the hall and the belly is the temple," this is precisely contemplating the mind.
The examples such as "cloud-colored halls" and "desiring to abandon" refer to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
From the section on the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*) onwards, all subsequent passages concern the contemplation of the mind.
Regarding the statement "the eight birds symbolize the eight types of conceit (*māna*)," it is simply that pride (*māna*) and arrogance (*mada*) differ in terms of subject and object.

The various teachings also explain pride (*māna*) by means of the seven types of pride; the explanation provided here is largely identical to that in the *Abhidharmakośa*, though its intent differs slightly, which I shall now briefly compare.
*Śaṅkha* (盛壯) is pride like *asmimāna* (我慢); its name and meaning are identical to those in the *Abhidharmakośa*. Because one is robust, one thinks "I am strong.
*Gotra* (姓) is pride like *mahāmāna* (大慢). The *Abhidharmakośa* says:

"To claim superiority over others who are superior. It is like a person of humble lineage who still does not yield to the Cui or Lu clans, or like an owl that still preys upon its mother—how much more so for one of noble lineage?
Pride born of wealth is a form of overweening conceit (*abhimāna*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"To consider oneself equal to others who are superior. How much less would one who is actually wealthy do so, when even a person of the world who is poor does not debase himself below Shi Chong?
The pride of self-sufficiency (*aiśvarya-māna*) is like false arrogance; as the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"To claim for oneself qualities that one does not possess among those who do possess them. If even those of meager fortune do not bow before those with virtue, how much less would those who possess power?
Pride regarding longevity is like overweening pride (*adhimāna*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"To claim one has attained what one has not attained. To reckon oneself as long-lived while presuming permanence is like a youth who is unwilling to respect the elderly; how much less so when one is actually advanced in years?
Intelligence-conceit (*medhā-mada*) is like pride (*māna*); as the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"To claim equality with others when one is equal to them, and to disparage those who are equal. If one wishes to disparage others even when one's own strength is inferior, how much more so when they are truly one's equals?
"Pride of practicing virtue" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-māna*) refers to being conceited regarding one's own goodness, whether it be superior or inferior. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"To consider oneself slightly inferior when one is largely superior. When one's virtues and deeds are separated by a vast gulf from those of the exalted, one might still claim to be only slightly below their lofty footsteps; how much more so, then, for one who is truly inferior?
Pride in physical form is like the pride of arrogance; as the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"To consider oneself equal when one's form is not superior to others. Even those who are unattractive do not willingly admit they are inferior to Pan An, let alone those with beautiful features.
To speak briefly, as the names differ, so it is here: these eight matters exist directly as they are, and thus those who possess arrogance (*māna*) do not necessarily possess all of them.

From the phrase "self-love is greed" (*ātmasnehaḥ lobhaḥ*) onward, the similarities and differences are further explained by analogy with the three poisons (*triviṣa*). Thus, each of the four contemplations (*cintā*) has two names, because the basis from which they derive their names is not fixed.

The creature is named for its animal-like appearance yet possesses the essence of a ghost and the form of a spirit; although this is not strictly essential, it may serve as a rough analogy for the messenger.
"Wuan" refers to the black snake.
Therefore, the *Hanshu* states:
"The 'xuánluán' and 'fù' [are venomous snakes]. The *Erya* states:

"The *huǐ* (viper) is three inches long and as thick as a finger"; in the region south of the Yangtze River, the *huǐ* is called a *fú* (cottonmouth), which has fangs and venom, with needle-like projections on its nose.
"The *wúgōng*" (centipede) is the *jíqū*.
Some say that those who can subdue snakes, or those who have tamed them, are mostly barefooted.
This statement is harmful, for it fails to consider the retribution that follows.
The "shou-gong" (lizard) is the *yanyan* (gecko). Some say:
when it is in a house it is called a shou-gong, and when it is in a marsh it is called a yanyan.
The character "𠯗" resembles a rat; if it refers to a beast, it is called "yòu," which resembles a monkey.
Regarding the character "yòu," the *Yùpiān* states:
"It resembles a wildcat and also eats rats; when it rains, it hangs upside down from trees, its tail having two forks to plug its two nostrils."
The character "lǐ" (badger/fox) in the *Shuowen Jiezi* is derived from "zhì" (beast).
As for "xī," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
"A small mouse."
The *Yupian* states:
"There is a venomous creature that stings humans and beasts; even when it has finished [stinging], there is no pain, and it is the 'sweet-mouthed rat' (*gan kou shu*).
'Jǔ' (咀) simply means to chew; 'bó' (摶) means to strike or beat."
“Grasping and clutching” means to seize; it also implies striking or stroking.

Regarding the phrase “affectionate love and greed,” etc., this is used here to contrast with the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*); the various views will be explained later among the spirits and deities, and they may also be considered sharp within the category of the dull.
If one speaks from the perspective of the dull faculty, the principle is likewise a principle for those of dull faculties.
"Investigation" serves as the explanation.

Just as the Confucian school of this land also posits such things as the Mandate of Heaven and vital energy (*qi*), which are all subsumed under the category of the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*), one would wish to compare them with the principles of the West [India], yet they are worlds apart.
"One says" [the following], which is a reiteration intended to provide a further explanation of the "dull afflictions" (*mṛdu-kleśa*).
As for "grabbing" (*zhā*), the *Shiming* states:
"It is 'to cross' (*chā*)."
This means grasping with all five fingers.
"Jie" (掣) means to pull.
It is also said to mean pulling forward or pulling backward.
Regarding "growling" (hēi-xī): the character "xī" is also written as "yí," which refers to pursing the lips and baring the teeth.
Regarding "howling and barking" (háo-fèi): it refers to letting out a loud, roaring sound.
In the *Sūtra*, "chimei" (魑魅) refers to the *jing* (essences/spirits) of things.
The *Tongsu Wen* states:
"The monsters of mountains and marshes are called *chi*."
The "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" (*Xijing fu*) states:
"The mountain deity with a tiger’s form is called a *chī*; the deity of the dwelling with a pig’s head and human form is called a *mèi*.
As for 'wǎngliǎng,' these are transformations and anomalies of wood and stone."
The *Yupian* states:
"A water deity.
Regarding "furnishing milk," the *Yupian* states:
"To incubate eggs is called *fu*.
The *Tongsuowen* says:
"To hatch from an egg is called *fu*."
The *Guangya* states:
"Fu also means 'to give birth.
'Nu' (breast-milk) means 'to nourish.'"
Therefore, it is said that birds hatch from their eggs (*fu*) and beasts give birth by lactation (*ru*).

Regarding the phrase "from their own kind" and so forth: this refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) obtaining a result of similar outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), which is illustrated by the analogy that a child resembles its father.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) consists of similar [dharmas] belonging to its own category (*nikāya*) and level (*bhūmi*), which have arisen previously. This refers to the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) and nine levels (*nava-bhūmi*); however, it concerns only the past acting as the cause for the present, as explained in detail in that text.
"Kumbhāṇḍa" refers to a fearsome ghost.
"Crouching" (dun) means sitting on one's heels;
"squatting" (ju) means sitting with the feet flat on the ground.

Regarding the subsequent passage on "seizing the dog" and so forth, because there is this particular interpretation, it is said "one version states. Seizing the dog's foot is like the cause [of slander], and seizing it is like the act of slandering; seizing the foot and striking it is like causing the sound to cease, which is why it says "causing him to lose his voice."

The nature of cause and effect is such that sound does not arise from the absence of grasping, but rather from the act of seizing and striking; it is like how birth occurs because of conceptualization.
As for the phrase "placing a foot upon the neck," because the sound did not cease, he again placed a dog's foot upon the dog's neck.

On top of denying the cause of suffering, one further repudiates the fruit of suffering; it is like placing a foot upon a neck, hoping that the sound will surely cease—yet how much more intense is that sound! To deny the fruit is even more severe than to deny the cause.

The phrase "Accumulating [karma] results in the attainment of its fruit" explains the preceding line: how could one possibly silence oneself by clutching a dog’s two paws? If you vainly slander the existence of cause and effect, how can you hope to escape the resulting retribution?

The phrase "denying the arising of suffering" below explains the latter part of the verse; it is like when one attempts to silence a sound by tightening the neck, yet the sound becomes even louder because of that very effort.
Furthermore, "denying the cause of suffering" refers specifically to the misconception of what is not a cause as being a cause, which is itself a form of denial.

That which was originally a mundane cause is now called a supramundane cause; this is because one would otherwise be slandering the existence of these two causes. Regarding "explanation through contemplation" (*guanjie*):
the previous explanation was based on phenomena (*shi*), which mostly pertained to the view of annihilationism, hence the use of terms such as "denying" (*bawu*).

The present explanation is based on contemplation (*guan*); its meaning encompasses both common and deviant views, as well as the correct and the false. Since there are also disciples of the Buddha who cultivate the contemplation of the six practices (*liuxing guan*), it is employed here.

If outsiders practice, they mostly calculate [existence] as eternal, or calculate the four dhyānas up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as eternal; this is because they hold them to be permanent.
Generally speaking, when it comes to contemplative understanding, one must accord with the internal [truth].
Furthermore, regarding the statement "producing impurity" and so forth, this meaning also takes the emission of sound as a fault; it arises due to contemplation, just as sound arises from striking.
As for the phrase "it should not arise now," this is explained by taking the cessation of sound as a fault; therefore, it is said that it does not arise.

Regarding the phrase "vertically entering" (*jūnyū*) and so forth: although there are various interpretations of the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*), they mostly concern the three periods of time—past, future, and present—or the transition from the present into the future; therefore, they are termed "vertical."

Regarding the phrase "transversely pervasive" (*pārśvato vyāpti*) and so forth: it is like the twenty types of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which consist of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the aggregates (*skandha*). Since these four propositions, when compared with one another, possess no further superiority or inferiority, they are termed "transverse."

Not cultivating wholesome dharmas constitutes such indulgence; thus, one does not cultivate them because of the denial [of their efficacy]. Although this is not a denial [of the dharmas themselves], it is still termed "lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*).

Regarding "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): it is the reckoning of what is not a fruit as being a fruit. That which is neither perception nor non-perception is not the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, yet one reckons it to be eternal.

The formless realm being "mind-only" is called "the throat is narrow"; the lifespan in the three realms reaching its limit is called "the life is precarious"; reckoning it as permanent is called "preserving the lifespan," which precisely corresponds to the meaning of reckoning the fruit.
The phrase "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) provides a further detailed explanation of the error of such a calculation.

Regarding the phrase "the head is like," etc.: the fundamental self is like an ox; just as the world regards the strength of an ox as supreme sovereignty (*maheśvara*), one calculates the self to be likewise. Furthermore, within that [self], one calculates its existence or non-existence, which is like the growth of two horns.
Regarding the phrase "the body is the self" and so forth: this concerns the mutual presence or absence of the self and the body.
"The body is the self" means grasping that which is acted upon as the self;
"the self is the body" means taking the agent as the object.

The body is that which belongs to the self (*ātmiya*), and the self is that which possesses it (*ātman*). For example, when one reckons among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that one aggregate is the self and the others are what belongs to the self—such as servants, ornaments, and dwellings—if one reckons [the self] as permanent, then the body is not the self; the body is subject to cessation while the self is permanent.
If one calculates in terms of annihilation, there is the annihilation of the body and the annihilation of the self, or both are considered eternally annihilated.

This is fully as explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* commentary, which cites the *Āgama* on the views of the past eons (*pūrvānta-dṛṣṭi*) and the views of the future eons (*aparānta-dṛṣṭi*). Although the subject and object of these calculations differ, their underlying principle of calculating existence is the same; or, in terms of temporal duration, these various non-Buddhists calculate the transitions within a single lifetime. The ultimate limit of their calculation reaches up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Taking what they calculate as the "head," they give rise to alternating calculations of permanence and annihilation within that stage, like tangled, disheveled hair.

Those who calculate permanence and so forth argue with one another over right and wrong; the strong subdue the weak, and the weak submit to the strong, all destroying others to follow themselves as if they were mutual predators.
To calculate this "self" as being either subject to annihilation or eternal is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the term "yakṣa" and so forth: the first two lines "summarize desire" without yet distinguishing between those of sharp and dull faculties; from "it is also" onwards, there is a further separate discussion regarding the meaning of sharp and dull faculties.
This also refers to the first two lines: that is, the upper line indicates the sharp-witted, and the lower line indicates the dull-witted.

The passage beginning with "All are with outflows" (*sāsrava*) explains the third line: because all minds with outflows lack the food of the flavor of the Path, they are hungry; and because they are hungry, they cycle through birth and death rapidly, which is why it is called "urgent."

Regarding the "four types of seekers" (*catur-yāna*) mentioned in the Sūtra: although the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are numerous, they do not exceed these four categories. Since both those of sharp and dull faculties possess the sense of being "hungry and urgent," the Sūtra’s text explains them here primarily from the perspective of the sharp-faculty afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-āsrava*).
"Peering through" (*kuìkàn*) means to look furtively and secretly. "Looking at what is not upright" refers to seeing through a window or lattice;

thus, one sees the void as partial, yet the void itself has no partiality or correctness—it is due to that window through which one peers. In principle, there is neither right nor wrong, yet those who harbor calculating thoughts commit an error. Therefore, it is said: "Those with many attachments do not comprehend the correct principle. Thus we know that regarding the heterodox and the orthodox, who does not each claim to admire the Ultimate Way? These two phrases collectively conclude the discussion of the two *anuśayas* (latent tendencies).
The following two lines summarize the extensive description and conclude the refutation.

Regarding the phrase "This dilapidated old house," the preceding text states, "Now these three realms are all mine. This is spoken from the perspective of the Transformation Master (the Buddha) as a whole, so that sentient beings may take up the [Pure] Land.
The term "dilapidated and old" is spoken with reference to [the house] from the time of its birth.

Therefore, in the preceding and following passages, the kingdom, city, household, and so forth—whether superior or inferior according to their respective contextual implications—are all connected to this "birth" and ultimately converge upon the elder; this applies to every single color and fragrance without exception.
"Householder," and below, explain the latter two phrases.
Regarding "internal correspondence" up to "should abandon the response," these two phrases are combined.

If one were to take the sixteen princes as the constant teaching, it should have been said that "the princes abandoned the response"; however, because this is now spoken from the perspective of the fruit, it says "Tathāgata."

Furthermore, since the abandonment of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense would not be solitary due to the presence of great impurity (*saṃkleśa*), we know that it is not merely the case that turbidity arises after the abandonment of the offense; rather, the abandonment of the offense occurs precisely because turbidity arises.

Therefore, one should know that the preceding passages concerning the arousal of turbidity, the salvation from the great fire, and the appropriate methods of transformation all derive their meaning from the later sections of the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Pervading) Sūtra.

According to this underlying principle, although the three cycles differ according to the higher or lower capacities of sentient beings, when one investigates their ultimate source, they are all without exception the same; thus, they may be applied universally.

Regarding "life span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*), it serves as an auxiliary to establish the proximate meaning; since the actual establishment is remote, it is established through the enumeration of intermediate stages. Establishment is itself emergence, and because this refers only to a single period of existence, "many" is not mentioned.
Furthermore, because it conceals the fundamental [nature], one cannot say that it is "many.

Regarding the phrase "the force of the fire's arising," both the perspectives of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) must be applied here as its characteristics.
One should know that, generally speaking, there are two kinds of power (*śakti*):
first, the power of domain (*pradeśa-śakti*), and second, the power of majesty (*anubhāva-śakti*).

The power of domain extends as far as the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), while the power of majesty incinerates all things without exception; now, the two powers of this realm are likewise so.

The dwelling is broad while the house is narrow: the triple world is the dwelling and the five aggregates are the house. If we take the desire realm as an illustration, the principle can be understood accordingly.
Because of turbidity and inversion, body and life are impermanent; thus, one should interpret this passage through the lens of impermanence.
The characteristics of being burned are divided into three meanings:

the first two phrases pertain to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the next one phrase pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); and the final three phrases clarify the reason why [the fire] does not go out.
Since this is specifically due to [the nature of] views, it is again called *piśāca*.
Furthermore, because the first two phrases list [beings] in general, it says "ghosts, spirits, and so forth," where "and so forth" includes insects and beasts.
The next line lists them individually; therefore, it further mentions "kumbhāṇḍas" and so forth.
In the second of the first two phrases, the latter clause specifically clarifies the characteristic of burning, hence it says "loudly crying out."

In the next line, the latter two phrases clarify that the ignorant do not know how to emerge; it is precisely because they do not emerge that they are burned, and because they are burned, they cannot emerge. Therefore, these are collectively categorized under the characteristic of burning.

Regarding the phrase "weeping is the raising of sound," this explains the present passage by means of the subsequent grief, lamentation, sorrow, and affliction within the twelve links [of dependent origination]. This is the ancient masters' interpretation that weeping and so forth pervade all three realms.

Now, as for not following the old interpretation: it simply means that within the human realm of the desire world, [the precept-attachment] exists only where there are established social conventions, and is not subsumed by other states.
"The attachment to precepts originally does not involve the calculation of annihilation," because it takes the cause as being equivalent to the fruit.

Among the categories burned by the fire arising in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the first two phrases refer to dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*) and the subsequent two phrases refer to sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). However, within the description of the fire's intensity, the text does not explicitly distinguish between sharp and dull; this must be explained through the underlying meaning. Thus, while such a distinction was not made for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), it is likewise absent here in the realm of form.
Next, we clarify that within the meditative signs (*nimitta*), there are both sharp and dull faculties, namely those involving "the subversion of signs" and so forth.

Since various views and delusions arise within dhyāna, one practices dhyāna while still possessing these views; thus, either the dhyāna has already ceased while the view arises, or the dhyāna and the view arise simultaneously. Whether it be the case that the dhyāna has already ceased while the view remains, or that both have been lost, [the practitioner remains bound].
Regarding "speculating on differences," this is fully illustrated by such views as those concerning past eons and past perspectives (*pūrvānta-dṛṣṭi*).

As for "silence," according to the Mahāyāna, silence is established within each of the dhyānas: for instance, silence is the sixth [limb] in the first dhyāna, and so on up to silence being the fifth [limb] in the fourth dhyāna; yet because they are attached to silence, they lose the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
According to other sūtras and śāstras, one regards attachment to dhyāna as silence, or regards a single factor of concentration (*ekāgra-citta*) as silence.

Regarding the statement, "The craving of the desire realm for future concentration has already been severed," this refers to the fact that although the nature of the obstruction has not yet been eliminated, its suppression is designated as "severance"; therefore, it is only when the time comes for the fierce beast to devour [the body] that it is truly called "exhausted."
Regarding the passage from "the desire realm" to "like a fierce flame," etc.: smoke and flames rise upward, yet because smoke surpasses the flames, it is used as a metaphor for form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, just as the flame is fierce while the smoke is subtle, so too is form light while desire is heavy.
Because the body and so forth pervade the two realms and the four inversions, it is said that they are "equal on all four sides.

Regarding the phrase "also pervades" (*yì tōng*) below, it may also serve as a dual metaphor for the two sets of four; thus, the four great elements, skin, and flesh occupy the four sides of the body, and because all four sides are entirely suffering, it is said they are "pervasive and filling" (*chōngsè*).
Regarding the phrase "under the centipede," which clarifies matters within the intermediate space (*ākāśa*): previously, dwelling in a hole was used as a metaphor for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);

now, because one has emerged from the hole, it is used as a metaphor for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The term "in the air" does not refer to empty space (*ākāśa*) itself; since the interior of a house was already used to metaphorize entry into the desire realm and the hole to metaphorize the form realm, the open ground outside the hole is now taken as "space" to metaphorize the formless realm. Thus, the form realm is like a hole; aversion to the lower [realms] is like being scorched by fire, while aspiration for the higher [realms] is like emerging from the hole.

Regarding the statement, "If that is so, hatred (dveṣa) pervades all three realms": previously, in the context of the desire realm, hatred was compared to a centipede; here, following that analogy, it is not distinguished separately. Since it has already been stated that the centipede is also formless (ārūpya), this serves as a metaphor for that hatred. Although there are no centipedes within the form realm (rūpadhātu), the mention of "poisonous insects" includes the centipedes; just as the mention of *piśācas* in the form realm includes all other types of ghosts, we know that hatred pervades all three realms.
In the Hīnayāna, it is said that there is no anger (*vyāpāda*) in the upper realms; however, this does not fully accord with the ultimate principle.

For although the various afflictions (*kleśa*) differ in their degree of gravity, they persist even up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); how much more so could they be excluded from the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?

However, although the names are the same, their referents differ; this principle must be distinguished. In the present case, the category of "that which is burned" essentially lacks spirits or deities (*bhūta*).
Regarding the phrase "if one attains," etc.: if, upon the arising of the formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one immediately gives rise to attachment, it is therefore called "following."

"Having already departed [from the lower realms]," they falsely conceive that the meditative absorption (samādhi) they rely upon is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana); therefore, it is said that "the fire burns upon the heads of all hungry ghosts.

Regarding the statement "neither-perception-nor-non-perception also possesses the eight sufferings," the text has already enumerated seven and lacks "separation from the beloved"; one should understand that the suffering experienced when losing the meditative absorption is what is termed "separation from the beloved."

However, regarding the first four of the seven sufferings mentioned in the text, they are designated as "moment-to-moment" (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*) because their essential nature arises as subtle perceptions that do not abide for even a single moment; the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death may be understood in the same way.
Next, there are two types of suffering explained in relation to cultivation; because one cultivates the higher [realms] and loses the lower ones, this is collectively termed "detachment.

Next, regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*), they are further categorized according to the fixed fruits [of the path]: the first four and the eighth are situated within the fruit.
Whether in terms of cause or fruit, both are defined by that samādhi; therefore, it may be so described.

Regarding the phrase "not dwelling in the foremost seat of emptiness": the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā) is conjoined with wisdom as its principle and is of the same essence as compassion. Now, it is said that one does not abide in wisdom devoid of compassion, but constantly dwells in compassion endowed with wisdom; hence, it is called "not dwelling."
Thus, one knows that compassion without conditions (anālambana-karuṇā) can only be of the same essence as wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "The old [commentary] says," how could the Buddha not know [this] and wait for another to inform him?
Regarding the phrase "It further says," how could there be any sentient being who would turn back and say to the Buddha, "You are my son"?
Even if there is a correspondence between response and stimulus, what is so wrong with regarding the arising [of the Buddha] as being for the sake of others?

However, when interpreting the scriptural passage concerning the words "hearing" and "existence," it would instead be like using a lower term to refer to a higher one; therefore, this approach is not adopted.
"Now, as for the explanation that follows": Generally speaking, the address "you" may be applied to the teacher, and the teacher is the Dharma.
Thus, both the other interpretation and the two principles mentioned above are established.
Question:

True Suchness (tathatā) and the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) may indeed be the Teacher of the Buddha; however, while the Samādhi of Contemplating Capacities may be called "Dharma," it merely illuminates the conventional (saṃvṛti). How, then, can it be called the Teacher?
Answer:
The one who contemplates belongs to wisdom, and wisdom is itself the Buddha.
Because he gives rise to illumination based on samādhi, he attains the status of this Teacher.

Although it is said that one observes according to capacity (*jī*), the essence of illumination is the Dharma; because it is like the Buddha-eye’s observation and so forth, it is only by possessing this eye that one can observe capacities. This meaning is like the process of "sending away" (or dispelling).

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, it says," this refers to the perspective of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). The interpretation of others is more proximate, while your own interpretation is somewhat more incisive; for when one considers unconditional compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*) in relation to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), unconditional compassion addresses the response-body, causing it to arise and transform sentient beings.

The phrase "and so forth" refers to the preceding section’s differentiation of distinctions and the loose intent regarding emerging from contemplation; it merely serves to allow the dharma and the analogy to be provisionally divided.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Questioning the Son's Origin," the two interpretations provided in the response skillfully capture both the facts and the underlying principle.

Regarding the initial response: although it has not yet emerged, its meaning resembles that which has already emerged; although it has not yet entered, its meaning resembles that which has subsequently entered. Because what has emerged is as yet unemerged, entry appears as though it has entered.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation from the perspective of understanding: it is "emergence" because of fundamental purity, and "entry" because of ignorance; yet, based on this meaning, one speaks of "emergence and entry" while actually being neither emerging nor entering.
In the explanation according to phenomena, after having regressed from the Mahāyāna, one takes the five desires as one's play;
in the explanation according to principle, one takes conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) as one's play.

What is called "proliferation" (*prapañca*) refers to the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the triple world. Because views and afflictions are identical to principle, they emerge from it; because principle is identical to views and afflictions, they enter into it.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, even the realization of the Small Vehicle is considered proliferation; thus it says:
"If one says, 'I shall perceive suffering, abandon its origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path,' this is proliferation and not the seeking of the Dharma."
Therefore, everything outside of true reality (dharmatā) is termed conceptual proliferation (prapañca).

Consequently, both the understanding of phenomena and the understanding of principle, although the great resolve was awakened during the time of Mahāvairocana Buddha, did not yet shatter ignorance; thus, they possess both the meanings of phenomena and principle.

In the section following "Great Goodness" (*mahākuśala*), the reasons for regression and the nature of attachment are explained. What was previously termed "unattached" (*anabhiniviṣṭa*) refers to those with shallow karmic connections; after regressing, they wander through saṃsāra possessing only ignorance, hence they are called "ignorant" (*ajñāna*). This interpretive meaning itself also encompasses two explanations, which can be seen upon reflection.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In the four and a half verses above, I shall... and so forth, this section on the "Instructional Gate" (誡門) regarding the "Appropriate Application" (擬宜) should be further divided as follows: the first verse-line correctly clarifies the appropriate application;
the next line establishes in general that which is to be burned, namely, the afflictions of views and thought (見思);
and the following line generally clarifies the power of the burning.
The next two lines briefly clarify the characteristics of burning;

the following one and a half lines extensively clarify that which is burned, wherein the two categories of *darśana-heya* (delusions abandoned through insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned through cultivation) are listed intermingled rather than in sequential order;
the final line concludes by means of an analogy, of which the first two phrases present the object of comparison and the subsequent two phrases provide the actual analogy itself.
Because they lack concentration and wisdom, they suffer from hunger and thirst, which are already terrifying; how much more so when they are further scorched by the fires of defilement?

Just as when one attains contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*) of the higher realms but lacks uncontaminated absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*), one is already burned by minor fires, let alone being cast down and scorched by the great fires of the desire realm. Hunger and thirst are precisely what constitute this suffering; therefore, one should seek the Mahāyāna to attain eternal liberation from it.
The three phrases following "all sons" mean that they do not receive [the teaching], which constitutes a lack of spiritual capacity (*amūka*); this is because they are immature and ignorant.
Since the text is abbreviated, it simply states "ignorant."

The *Sūtra* states, "They still take pleasure in and remain attached [to them]. This means that they neither possess great aspirations nor practice the minor [vehicles]; having abandoned both the great and the small, they nevertheless remain attached to the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Next, regarding "the third phrase: properly ceasing the transformation," this means that because [sentient beings] do not abandon their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the Great Transformation is suspended. Even if they do not abandon their views and afflictions, they may still possess the great capacity (*mahā-yogya*); at such a time, the Tathāgata does not begrudge the Great [Vehicle]. However, because both the Great and Small [vehicles] would be lost [if he did not act], and they possess only views and afflictions, he provisionally causes them to emerge from the turbidity through one of two paths, first bestowing the Small [Vehicle].
Regarding the phrase "the first three verses outline the intent": the first verse clarifies the purpose of the outline;
the subsequent verse explains the reason for employing the Lesser Vehicle—namely, that because [beings] are attached to views and afflictions, only the Lesser Vehicle is bestowed upon them.

Next, regarding the intention of using a small portion of the half-line: if one does not employ the small, then both the large and the small perish; therefore it is said that they will be harmed by fire. Because of this harm, the body is lost; because the body is lost, life is forfeited.

Next, regarding the "half-verse" on correct reflection using small [vehicles], the *Sūtra*’s mention of "wondrous jewels" (*miao bao*) still pertains to the provisional means (*upāya*), as in the case of "subtle cessation, subtle detachment," or the *Āgama*’s description of them as "the most wondrous among the wondrous. If these wondrous jewels were the Great [Vehicle], why would they all go to their father’s place to request vehicles?

Regarding the "Manifestation of Turning" (*saṃdarśana-parivarta*), the *Sūtra* states that they were "outside the gate. This is like demonstrating the Four Noble Truths to bring about knowledge of the supramundane; thus, in the "Reiterated Exhortation," it says, "Come forth! This exhorts them regarding the mode of practice: one must contemplate the Truths in order to emerge from the house.
