Regarding the subsequent proof of the transformation, the meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: "I am skilled at constructing chariots to provide for all; by this, it is verified that I shall certainly not lack chariots myself. By citing his own experience, he proves there is no error, and by the evidence of his own granting, he proves it is not in vain. Therefore, one knows that he uses the very chariots he himself employs to exhort others so that they may obtain them.
Taking oneself as an example for others, it is therefore said to be "outside.
When the *Sūtra* speaks of the "four crossroads," this refers to the Four Noble Truths.
My previous refusal to interpret them as the four turbidities was based on this underlying meaning.
Regarding the phrase "initially standing outside the gate": because the eldest son was still within, the father remained standing; now that the son has emerged, he sits at ease.

Furthermore, because the great capacity for conversion had not yet been met, he is said to be "standing"; because the minor transformation has already been completed, he "sits at ease. Thus, one knows that "standing" refers to benefit through the unmanifest, while "sitting" refers to benefit through the manifest.
Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* that says, "He spoke to himself in celebration," and so forth: he rejoices because he has found the sentient beings who are to be converted.
Since those two hundred trillion Buddhas had instructed him regarding this great causal condition (*mahā-pratyaya*), it is said, "it was born."
Because they have reached a small degree of maturity during this intermediate stage, it is called "nurturing" (*yù*).
Having passed through this long period and being matured repeatedly, because they are difficult to sustain and nourish, it is said to be "extremely difficult."
Because the great is subtle and the small is foolish, turbidity arises from ignorance; since causes invite their effects, it is said "entering the house.
The two lines following "many various" in the *Sūtra* describe the fires of the views and afflictions that have arisen.
The passage in the *Sūtra* beginning with "Great Fire" describes the intensity of the flames that consume [the world].
The passage in the *Sūtra* beginning with "And this" correlates [this fire] with the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*).
The passage in the *Sūtra* beginning with "I have already... clarifies the cause for their joy.
The passage beginning with "For this reason... concludes the sentiment of joy.

Regarding the three lines beginning with "Knowing [him as] his father," which describe the request for the carriage: the first two lines clarify the time of the request for the carriage, providing evidence that the aforementioned person sitting there is indeed the father.
The next two lines constitute the actual request (*yācanā*), and the following two phrases conclude the request.
Within the actual request, the first line is the formal request itself, while the second line describes the granting of permission.

Regarding the statement in the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* from "the aforementioned text" up to "there should be five types of mentalities": there is no separate explanation for the "combined" mentality; furthermore, within the verse, the "combined" mentality is not expanded upon. Since the "equal chariot" (or equal vehicle) is already present, one must necessarily understand the various mentalities.
Regarding the statement, "The faculties (*indriya*) possess all dharmas and are called 'treasuries' (*kośa*)," this is explained solely in terms of their capacity for containment.

Regarding the statement, "The six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) possess all dharmas and are called 'storehouses' (*koṣṭha*)," while the treasury is broad and the storehouse is narrow, they may also be discussed interchangeably, and so forth.

It is merely according to the different repositories in which they are stored; for although the faculties (indriya) are each distinct, they are each complete within themselves. Thus, all formations (saṃskāra) are complete within the various faculties. Since formations pervade the faculties, both the faculties and the formations are complete with all dharmas; this is what is meant by being "near" to the profound treasury.

Just as when traveling a long distance, one's roots may be shallow; yet whether far or near, all possess the various dharmas, and when considering practice in relation to the roots, there is no further distinction.

Were it not for the precedent of certain schools who, relying on the sūtras, have composed commentaries and sub-commentaries, how could one hear this teaching that both the roots and the practice constitute the treasury and the storehouse, each fully containing all dharmas?

Regarding the "intention within the great vehicle" in the Sūtra: all that pertains to cause and effect is collectively termed "various jewels. In terms of the meaning of attaining through the cultivation of the teaching, it is like "creation"; yet because the nature and cultivation differ, it is expediently termed "creation. Because there are many practices and many offspring, the vehicles are not one; therefore, that which is created is manifold and moreover vast.

Furthermore, one must demonstrate the directions so that it may be known that the name "cultivation" (xiū) is actually "construction" (zào); because cultivation and construction are extinguished in their nature, they return to what is originally possessed, which is the very body of the chariot.
The phrase "adorned and decorated" below refers to the complete perfections (pāramitās).
The first line is explained as before.
When the *Sūtra* mentions "pearls" and so forth, it describes the characteristics of the canopy.
The gates of compassion are not one; they are like the mesh of a net, with a single pearl within each opening, just as all the various gates of compassion correspond to reality.

The preceding text merely states that "various flower tassels hang down," which simply means causing those who see them to rejoice; the present text says they "hang down everywhere," thereby clarifying that all capacities for awakening are universally gladdened.
The *Sūtra* states, "Various colors," and so forth. The first phrase clarifies that while the places where the transformative influence descends may differ according to what is appropriate;
the second phrase clarifies that in the suitability for gathering sentient beings, there is nothing lacking.

The *Sūtra* states that "soft and supple" (*mṛdusnigdha*) means that whereas previously it simply said "laid down in layers," here it adds the praise "soft and supple. Furthermore, it is covered with precious cotton cloth (*karpāsa*). Because one has mastery over all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), it is called "soft and supple"; it surpasses the coarse with its excellence, like a fine covering placed upon [the coarse].
Regarding the term "mattress" (*yin*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
"The layered mats within a carriage.
Because his practice of the dhyāna of complete fulfillment differs from that of ordinary or inferior practitioners, it is described as "fresh, white, pure, and clean."

Regarding the passage "wandering crosswise" (*yōgyū*) and so forth within the *Jikeshōkanpishō* (Notes on the Joy of Attaining the Vehicle), it means that although all phenomena reside within a single practice and each phenomenon is fully endowed with both the provisional and the real, even when they are unified, the four characteristics remain distinct and clear.

From the "four gates" to the "forty-one stages," as fully explained in the *Fashou Liyi Sishi* (The Four Explanations of the Principle of the Single Dharma), the meanings of the two explanations regarding the stages and the gates have already been established. The remaining two have already been discussed as previously stated; according to the intent of the above explanation, there is fundamentally no distinction between horizontal and vertical, though the meaning is divided into four aspects.

Now it is also like this: fundamentally there is neither horizontal nor vertical, yet by relying on the positions of the gates, one speaks of horizontal and vertical. Furthermore, "truth" (*di*) refers here to wisdom; whereas previously [the four virtues] were considered from the perspective of the illuminating subject, now they are considered from the perspective of that which is relied upon. Compared to the former, this only lacks the single element of the contemplative mind; when the four ultimate virtues are realized, this is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The "ninefold world" refers simply to the nine realms (*dhātu*).

When seven are compared to nine, one merely excludes the four *gatis* and separates the Bodhisattvas; because the sense of being a "child" [of the Buddha] applies universally, the world consists of nine, whereas because the sense of being "connected by affinity" is restricted, the provisional means (*upāya*) consist of only seven.

The *Sūtra* states, "All sentient beings are my children. As it says in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, there are no sentient beings who do not ultimately attain Great Parinirvāṇa. The meaning of "child" pertains to the cause, while Nirvāṇa pertains to the fruit; among the essential tenets of the Mahāyāna, none surpass these two. Since both are universally affirmed as existing, how can one follow provisional teachings and claim that a portion of them are non-existent?
The *Sūtra* states that "the mind devoid of wisdom" refers generally to the absence of reality.
Regarding the section on "various sufferings," the first two lines provide a general heading, the next two lines offer an explanation, and the final two lines provide a conclusion.
When the *Sūtra* says "tranquil," and so forth, it refers to the application of wisdom within the King Samādhi, which is precisely what constitutes abiding in peace.
When the *Sūtra* says "non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas," the meaning of "non-retrogression" is universal, encompassing even the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, and so on.

Regarding the statement, "In the prose [narrative], it is not appropriate to include both 'seeking' and 'joyful satisfaction,'" this is because 'avoiding calamity' is paired with 'seeking,' and 'equal bestowal' is paired with 'joy.

As for why, within the [four] sections, only the latter two are appropriate while the former two are not: among these four parts, 'avoiding calamity and seeking the vehicle' serves as the secondary element, whereas 'bestowing great joyful satisfaction' is the primary element.
The third section, beginning with "Although I... and consisting of one line and a half, further contains two parts:
the first line clarifies the removal of obstacles, and the subsequent half-line fulfills the original intention.

The second section, beginning with "If a person of small wisdom... and consisting of seven lines, fully encompasses the Four Noble Truths: the first two lines clarify the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); the next two lines clarify the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); the following line clarifies the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); the next half-line explicitly clarifies the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); and the final one and a half lines clarify that liberation through these four truths is not ultimate.

Within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), the first phrase indicates the cause for explaining suffering: because of limited wisdom (*parīttajñāna*), there is only mundane knowledge (*laukikajñāna*) capable of explaining only the minor [aspects].
The subsequent phrase clarifies that because the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*) is weighty, the Truth of Suffering must be elucidated.
The next line reiterates the cause of suffering;
the following line correctly clarifies the teaching on suffering.

The subsequent passage beginning with "The minds of sentient beings rejoice" explains the accordance with their original practice; therein, the first two lines clarify the capacity (the *mārga*), and the following two lines clarify the response (the *dharmaparyāya*).
Regarding the statement "there is no difference" within the middle [section]: as the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (or *Yìjiào jīng*) says, "True suffering cannot be made into pleasure.

Next, in the exposition of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), the first line correctly clarifies the Truth of Origination; the subsequent half-line reveals the remedy for the Truth of Origination; and the final half-line clarifies the faults and afflictions of origination.

Next, in the explanation of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), the first half-verse clarifies the function of ceasing the origin of suffering (*samudaya*); the next half-verse clarifies the attainment of its name; the subsequent section clarifies that liberation is not ultimate; therein, the first half-verse reiterates the attainment of liberation, while the following two lines beginning with "This person" constitute the inquiry.
Regarding the statement, "Attaining liberation through the contemplation of the truths—what kind of liberation is this?
the section beginning with "Merely detached" explains detachment from the realms of existence (*dhātu-bandhana*), clarifying only a limited liberation.

Following the section beginning with "In reality," three verses explain [this further]: the first one and a half lines use the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Way to refute [the limited view], while the subsequent one and a half lines reveal the Buddha’s original intent.
Regarding the clarification of the "categories of evil," the current text merely speaks of their being taught or not taught.
Some divide this section as follows:
first listing the causes of evil, followed by listing the results of evil.
There are fourteen causes of evil: first, arrogance; second, indolence;

third, conceiving of a self; fourth, shallow understanding; fifth, attachment to desire; sixth, lack of comprehension; seventh, lack of faith; eighth, frowning with displeasure; ninth, doubt; tenth, slander; eleventh, slighting the good; twelfth, hating the good; thirteenth, envying the good; and fourteenth, resenting the good.
Next, regarding the evil retributions, the first part provides an explanation, while the second part, beginning with "Śāriputra," consists of two lines that serve as a conclusion.

The former section also has two parts: the first clarifies how one falls into the evil realms due to slander; the second, beginning with "In this way," clarifies that because of falling into the evil realms, one is unable to encounter a Buddha.

The initial section also has three parts. First, regarding the hells, there is an extensive account of untimely [retribution]. While this division of the text is not without its underlying intent, it lacks a specific rationale.

Next, within the section on animals, the phrase "severing the seeds of the Buddha" refers precisely to destroying the two causes—the conditional (*pratyaya*) and the direct (*hetu*). Thus, while the preceding text speaks of severing the seeds of the Buddha in all worldly realms, this sutra universally opens the way for the Buddha-seeds in all six destinies; if one slanders this sutra, it is logically equivalent to severing them.
Question:
If slandering the sūtras gives rise to sin, is it not the case that the sūtra itself is the condition for the sin?
Answer:

Sin and merit arise from the mind; the scriptures merely serve as supporting conditions. This is like the formation of the body through the increase or decrease of the four great elements. However, according to the Buddha’s original intent, [the purpose] was solely to generate merit; thus, this is the fault of the deluded, not the blame of the path.

The three types of base persons are again divided into three in the subsequent text: first, it clarifies those who do not encounter a Buddha; second, those who again enter the evil realms; and third, those who again obtain human birth.
*Fahua Wenju Ji*, Fascicle Six, Part Two.
